newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr subdued as decision day nears.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr subdued as decision day nears.

text.p: The Australian dollar had to lean on support through a subdued Monday session, burdened as it was by the weight of speculation about a cut in domestic rates.

Weeks of second guessing have boiled down to this Tuesday's monthly meeting of the Reserve Bank board and it was rare to find anyone in the market not tipping a 0.5 point reduction in official rates to 6.5 percent come Wednesday morning.

So well discounted is a move, however, that analysts felt the real thing might prove a relief. "A cut looks on for one and all," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia. "But I have a feeling the AUD may rally once it's out the way."
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar had settled at US$0.7883/88, up slightly from an early US$0.7875 low but still off from Friday's late US$0.7896/01.
It also faded on the crosses to hit 89.15/25 yen from 89.60/70 late Friday and 58.2 in trade weighted terms after a 58.4 finish last week.

Traders said the currency had been smothered by profit taking while US$/yen retreated to 113.10 today from a 44-month peak of 114.92 less than a week ago. Recent samurai demand out of Tokyo also tapered off today as Japan was on holiday, but there was much talk of more issues in the pipeline this week.

At least five yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds were launched last week worth a total 135 billion yen, suggesting Japanese investors remained keen on the dollar's yield even though a cut in short term rates had been well discounted.

Money market and bond rates have already eased to reflect a 0.5 point cut but Japanese bond yields had also fallen sharply in recent weeks, so dealers saw little reason why the dollar should suffer greatly if one came about.
However, there were worries the RBA might ease by 75 basis points or more given a recent run of weak domestic data and they suspected the dollar could break lower in such a case.
Strong support was seen at US$0.7850/55, a trough reached in both September and October, and a breach there would risk a deeper retracement to key support at US$0.7810.
A bounce above US$0.7915 was needed to counter the immediate bearish outlook, and the currency would have to rally all the way past US$0.7985 to restore confidence in its old uptrend.
The case for a larger cut in interest rates, or perhaps even a series of them, had grown as release after release proved softer than expected and today's figures were no exception.
The ANZ job advertisements series, which measures job ads in the major Australian newspapers, fell 1.0 percent in October.
That followed losses of 0.4 in September and 2.3 percent in August and left ads at their lowest level since January 1994.

The decline in the trend rate did slow a little to 0.8 percent from 1.3 percent in September, but ANZ said the measure still pointed to average jobs growth of only 10,000 a month -- not enough to reduce the unemployment rate.
When the RBA last cut rates, on July 31, it emphasised its responsibility for reducing unemployment as a reason for the move, but the jobless rate had actually risen since then.
Meanwhile, inflation and wages growth had slowed sharply, retail sales had slumped and exports had tailed off.
"I can't see any reason for ther RBA not to go," said Roberts at UBS.

"Indeed, given that inflation has fallen and the AUD is likely to gallop higher if the RBA doesn't cut this week, you could argue that no move would represent a de-facto tightening in policy; and that's the last thing they should want," he said.

Bulls could take some comfort in the lastest data from the U.S. which pointed to a similar slowdown in growth there. That lessened the chance of the Federal Reserve hiking its interest rates this year and promised to keep the local currency's yield premium that little bit larger. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
